statements.text: Thank you for that. Dr. Bowne, in your experience have you find that AI-enabled tools used by law enforcement are tested and evaluated before they are deployed to ensure that they are safe and effective?
statements.context: Question posed by Representative Lucy McBath during a congressional hearing titled "Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk."

statements.text: Mr. Venzke, I want to go back to something that you did touch on though. You did touch on the moratorium on State and local AI, which actually failed. That last attempt failed. The Republican Chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee has already vowed to continue to pursue it even as they acknowledge that Federal legislation setting standards on AI is still years away. As we work to develop that legislation what principles or proposals should we consider?
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled 'Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk', where Rep. McBath questions a witness about federal AI legislative strategy.

statements.text: Mr. Venzke, how does the use of AI-enabled facial recognition comply with the Fourth Amendment's equal protection principles?
statements.context: Congressional hearing titled "Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk," during a question-and-answer round with witnesses.

statements.text: This is just so interesting you should say that because even on my phone I have facial recognition and sometimes it says I don't recognize you and I am like, well, you know who I am. Of course, there are still problems with AI and the technology still needs to be advanced. [...] Mr. Venzke, I am going to ask you another question: What warrant requirements and limitations should be applied for facial recognition tools when they are used by law enforcement?
statements.context: House hearing titled "Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk."

statements.text: Dr. Bowne, [...] how can public agencies use the procurement process to ensure that the AI systems they want to acquire are safe and effective?
statements.context: Question posed during a House subcommittee hearing titled 'Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk.'

statements.text: That is why it is critical that we proceed thoughtfully and put appropriate guardrails in place so that everyone in our criminal justice system that is using AI-enabled tools, they are using them responsibly, not to the detriment of law-abiding members of our community.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing 'Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk'

statements.text: Many cities and states have put sensible guardrails in place to limit potentially harmful uses of AI. That is why it was alarming when some of my Republican colleagues recently attempted to pass a moratorium on State and local AI regulations in the big ugly bill, a move that generated bipartisan opposition so much that 40 State Attorney Generals and 17 Republican Governors, including the Governor of my State, Georgia, wrote letters to the Senate in opposition to the proposed moratorium.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing 'Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk'

statements.text: I stand with those seeking to protect the health and the safety and civil rights of our communities from the abuses of AI and I hope that we can come together and follow the lead of the States to explore what those guardrails should look like and put them in place.
statements.venue: Opening statement, House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing 'Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Exploitation: A New Era of Risk'

statements.text: There are gaps in legislation. There are gaps in things that we need to do here in Congress to make sure that there are protections that are enforcing and preventing these kinds of deepfakes and all that we are talking about today.
statements.venue: Questioning of witnesses, House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and criminal exploitation

statements.text:
As more and more of our world becomes familiar with AI, it’s important that @EdWorkforceDems and Congress help keep Americans safe and informed.

Hear how kindergarteners in Georgia are enriching their learning 🎥 https://t.co/UP21EFvrdK

Artificial intelligence, or AI, as we know it, will be a part of that future, as my colleague Rep. Allen has stated. But we must act with caution and responsibility to ensure that these new technologies are working for regular people, working for all people, not making it more difficult for them to get good jobs and to keep those jobs.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, House Education & Workforce field hearing in Augusta, GA

statements.text: Some employers have used AI as a weapon in retaliation against workers who are unionizing or to lower wages. The unrestricted use of AI can also infringe on workers’ privacy and make it harder for workers to prove that their gender, race, age, or disability status were used to discriminate against them— which, despite all of the progress we have made in this country, unfortunately still happens every day.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, House Education & Workforce field hearing in Augusta, GA

statements.text: Congress must also not ignore the very real concerns that families across our country and in Georgia have about the expansion of data centers. Ansley Brown and her family in Coweta County were one of many forced to sell their family home— which will be demolished to make way for a power line to feed AI data centers. As AI continues to grow at a rapid pace, we have a responsibility to ensure that innovation— yes, we need innovation— but we have a responsibility to ensure that it does not come at the expense of the people it is meant to serve.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, House Education & Workforce field hearing in Augusta, GA

statements.text: Congress has a responsibility to rein in big tech companies so that AI can be used for Americans instead of being used against them. Many cities and states have put sensible guardrails in place to protect people and ensure AI is being used and expanded appropriately.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, House Education & Workforce field hearing in Augusta, GA

statements.text: What the American people do need is for Congress to take an active role in shaping how AI is integrated into our daily lives and in developing thoughtful regulations that balance protecting people with the need for economic growth.
statements.venue: Opening remarks, House Education & Workforce field hearing in Augusta, GA

statements.text: Yes, we need the innovation, but we have a responsibility to make sure that it does not come at the expense of the people it is meant to serve, [...] The future of AI is definitely promising, but it must also be guided by fairness, respect for people's homes, and a commitment to protecting families in Georgia and the communities they have built and lived in for generations.
